items.title: A tumour is a tiny evolving ecosystem
items.claim: Cancer cells accumulate mutations. Cells with mutations that confer growth advantages dominate. Drug treatment kills the susceptible cells but spares resistant ones — which then dominate the regrown tumour.
items.prompt: Why is cancer so hard to cure even with effective drugs?

options.text: Drugs don't work on cancer cells

A tumour contains millions to billions of slightly genetically different cells; selection pressure from a drug acts on the existing variation and rapidly enriches resistant clones — the same evolutionary process as antibiotic resistance, but inside a single patient

items.reveal_title: Tumour heterogeneity and the cost of monotherapy
items.reveal:
Single-cell sequencing of tumours reveals enormous clonal diversity. A 5 cm tumour may contain 10 to the 9 cells, each with its own profile of acquired mutations. Subclones can have different drug sensitivities, growth rates and metastatic potentials.

Treating with a single targeted therapy selects for whichever cells are pre-existingly resistant. Within months, the tumour regrows — now dominated by the resistant subclone. Combination therapy (targeting multiple pathways at once) makes resistance much less likely, by analogy with HIV's HAART protocol.

The Peter Nowell paper (1976) first proposed clonal evolution in cancer. Recent decades have made it the dominant framework, with implications for drug strategy, biomarker design, and the inevitability of resistance.
items.why: Cancer is taught as one disease. It's an evolving population of cells subject to selection — making it as much an ecological and evolutionary problem as a medical one.

items.title: Bees die when they sting — and this makes evolutionary sense
items.claim: A worker bee that stings a mammal disembowels itself and dies. Sterile, suicidal workers shouldn't exist if natural selection works at the individual level. They do exist, abundantly.
items.prompt: How does evolution favour individuals that don't reproduce?

options.text: Natural selection doesn't really work for social insects

Hamilton's rule: a gene for altruism spreads if rB is greater than C (relatedness times benefit exceeds cost); worker bees share 75 percent of their genes with sisters due to haplodiploidy, so helping the queen reproduce passes on their own genes effectively
Queen bees control workers chemically against their interests

items.reveal:
W. D. Hamilton wrote the equation rB greater than C: a gene for helping behaviour spreads if the relatedness (r) times the benefit to the recipient (B) exceeds the cost to the actor (C).

In haplodiploid Hymenoptera (bees, ants, wasps), females are diploid (from a diploid mother and a haploid father), males are haploid (unfertilised eggs). A worker shares 50 percent of her genes with her own offspring (if she had any), but 75 percent with her full sisters — because their shared father is haploid and gave them ALL his genes.

So a worker's gene-propagation interest is best served by helping her mother (the queen) make more sisters. Sterility is rational from the gene's perspective.

Hamilton's work, building on J. B. S. Haldane's quip 'I would lay down my life for two brothers or eight cousins', founded sociobiology.
items.why: Selection is taught as acting on individuals. The gene's-eye view explains altruism, sociality and self-sacrifice — phenomena that the individual-level view can't easily handle.

items.title: Eyes have evolved independently more than 40 times
items.claim: Eyes are complicated. Darwin worried about them in Origin of Species. Modern phylogenetics shows that eyes — from basic photoreceptors to full image-forming structures — have evolved independently somewhere between 40 and 60 times across animal lineages.
items.prompt: What does this tell us about evolution?

options.text: Eyes are too complex to evolve once, let alone many times

Photoreception is selected for so strongly that wherever a workable starting point exists (a light-sensitive protein) selection assembles eyes; complex outcomes evolve repeatedly when the gradient of advantage is steep
All eyes descend from a single ancestor
Vision is impossible without divine design

items.reveal_title: Eyes as evolutionary stress-tests for gradualism
items.reveal:
Modern eyes include: vertebrate camera eyes, cephalopod camera eyes (independently evolved, no blind spot), trilobite calcite-lens compound eyes, scallop mirror eyes, copepod parabolic-reflector eyes, jumping-spider sharp-focus eyes, brittle-star whole-body lensed skin.

Nilsson and Pelger (1994) modelled the evolution of a vertebrate-style camera eye from a flat patch of photoreceptors. With realistic mutation rates and selection coefficients of 1 percent, they estimated 400,000 generations — about half a million years — to produce a fully functional eye.

The common element across all 40+ origins: opsin proteins. The receptor molecules are conserved; the architectures around them have been built and rebuilt many times.
items.why: Eyes feel like such complex organs that they 'must' be hard to evolve. They are exactly the kind of thing selection invents many times when given a good starting molecule.
